steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper DCVNet on fast optical flow with dilated cost volumes. Introduce optical flow, how deep networks for it developed, why cost volumes with large displacements are expensive and handled sequentially, and then present our approach and its speed.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Optical flow: definition, history, applications
- Deep networks for optical flow and the cost volume
- Large displacements: sequential coarse-to-fine / RNN processing
- Our approach: dilated cost volumes processed once
- Comparison with PWC-Net and RAFT; speed

  - concatenate; simple convolutional network (U-Net) processes once

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Optical flow is a dense matching problem, and it is about estimating the displacement of every single pixel between two consecutive video frames, which captures the motion of brightness patterns. It is a classical problem in computer vision that has been studied for a long time, going back to the early 1980s. Optical flow is used in a wide range of other problems, for example scene flow estimation, action recognition, and video editing and synthesis.

Like for many other computer vision problems, the state-of-the-art approaches for optical flow estimation are all based on deep neural networks. But in the beginning, deep neural networks for optical flow reported worse results than the traditional well-engineered energy minimization approaches. To close the performance gap, one approach stacked several networks to increase capacity, which gave significant accuracy improvements. But increasing the capacity of the network led to huge networks and slower inference. Starting from one earlier approach, more and more classical principles from traditional optical flow estimation approaches were put into the design of neural networks, and this allowed deep neural networks to be more accurate than traditional approaches. In particular the cost volume, which is a more discriminative representation for optical flow than concatenated feature representations of the two images, is now an essential component of state-of-the-art approaches.

- Large displacements
  - cost volume needs neighborhood sampling; big neighborhood -> huge volume, heavy computation
  - small neighborhoods + sequential processing; coarse-to-fine pyramid with warping
  - full-range cost volume in recent work, but RNN only processes partial volume per recurrence
- Our approach
  - cost volumes with different dilation rates at the same time; small neighborhood captures small + large displacements
  - concatenate, U-Net processes once; interpolation weights -> flow; extra loss on weights
- Comparison
  - vs PWC-Net and RAFT: simpler, no sequential processing (Fig. 1)
  - comparable error; 30 fps on Sintel-resolution (1024\times 436), mid-end 1080ti GPU
  - code and weights released

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Optical flow is a dense matching problem, and it is about estimating the displacement of every single pixel between two consecutive video frames, which captures the motion of brightness patterns. It is a classical problem in computer vision that has been studied for a long time, going back to the early 1980s. Optical flow is used in a wide range of other problems, for example scene flow estimation, action recognition, and video editing and synthesis.

Like for many other computer vision problems, the state-of-the-art approaches for optical flow estimation are all based on deep neural networks. But in the beginning, deep neural networks for optical flow reported worse results than the traditional well-engineered energy minimization approaches. To close the performance gap, one approach stacked several networks to increase capacity, which gave significant accuracy improvements. But increasing the capacity of the network led to huge networks and slower inference. Starting from one earlier approach, more and more classical principles from traditional optical flow estimation approaches were put into the design of neural networks, and this allowed deep neural networks to be more accurate than traditional approaches. In particular the cost volume, which is a more discriminative representation for optical flow than concatenated feature representations of the two images, is now an essential component of state-of-the-art approaches.

To build the cost volume, we need to sample pairs of locations between the two input images in a neighborhood along both the horizontal and vertical directions and compute their similarity (or cost). A big neighborhood is needed to capture large displacements, but this gives a very large cost volume and a big computational burden. So most existing models capture large displacements sequentially, using cost volumes with small neighborhoods to be computationally efficient. Specifically, the coarse-to-fine strategy is widely used in state-of-the-art advances, where a pyramid is built based on the feature hierarchy of deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). In each pyramid level the optical flow estimated in the previous level is used to construct the cost volume with the warping operation. In recent ground-breaking work a full-range cost volume is constructed, but a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) is used to process only a partial cost volume with a small neighborhood at each recurrence, so large displacements are still captured sequentially.

In this paper we propose an alternative to these approaches, which does not use the sequential estimation strategy for processing the cost volume. Instead, we construct cost volumes with different dilation rates at the same time. Even with a small search neighborhood, small and large displacements can both be captured at once. We concatenate these cost volumes and then a simple convolutional network (a U-Net) processes the dilated cost volumes only once to get the optical flow. Specifically, we estimate the interpolation weights between all the possible displacements captured in the dilated cost volumes to get the optical flow. Besides the loss for the optical flow, we also design a loss term to supervise the interpolation weights better, which leads to better accuracy.

Compared to other approaches, like PWC-Net and RAFT, our approach is conceptually simpler and it does not need sequential processing of the cost volumes, as shown in Fig. 1. It gets comparable error rates on standard benchmarks, but our approach runs significantly faster at inference time, reaching 30 fps (frames per second) for a Sintel-resolution image (with a size of 1024\times 436) on a mid-end 1080ti GPU. We will make our code and the model weights publicly available.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Optical flow, as a dense matching problem, is about estimating each pixel's displacement between two consecutive video frames, capturing the motion of brightness patterns. It is a classical and long-studied problem in computer vision, dating back to the early 1980s [1]. Optical flow has applications in a wide range of other problems, such as scene flow estimation [2], action recognition [3], and video editing and synthesis [4].

As with many other computer vision problems, state-of-the-art approaches for optical flow estimation are all based on deep neural networks. Initially, however, deep neural networks for optical flow reported inferior results compared to traditional well-engineered energy minimization approaches [5]. To reduce the performance gap, one approach stacked multiple networks to increase capacity [6], resulting in significant accuracy improvements, but at the cost of huge networks and slower inference. Starting from [7], more and more classical principles derived from traditional optical flow estimation approaches were incorporated into neural network design, allowing deep neural networks to surpass traditional approaches in accuracy. In particular, the cost volume, a more discriminative representation for optical flow than concatenated feature representations of two images, is now an essential component of state-of-the-art approaches.

To build the cost volume, we need to sample pairs of locations between the two input images in a neighborhood along both horizontal and vertical directions and compute their similarity (or cost). A big neighborhood is required to capture large displacements, but it leads to a very large cost volume and a significant computational burden. Consequently, most existing models capture large displacements sequentially, using cost volumes with small neighborhoods for computational efficiency. Specifically, the coarse-to-fine strategy is widely adopted in state-of-the-art advances [8,9,10,11], where a pyramid is built on the feature hierarchy of deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), and in each pyramid level the optical flow estimated in the previous level is used to construct the cost volume with the warping operation. Although the recent ground-breaking work [12] constructs a full-range cost volume, a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) is employed to process only a partial cost volume with a small neighborhood at each recurrence, capturing large displacements sequentially.

In this paper, we propose an alternative to these prevailing approaches that does not use the sequential estimation strategy to process the cost volume. Instead, cost volumes with different dilation rates are constructed simultaneously, so that even with a small search neighborhood, both small and large displacements can be captured at once. After concatenating such cost volumes, a simple convolutional network (a U-Net) processes the dilated cost volumes only once to obtain the optical flow. Specifically, we estimate the interpolation weights between all possible displacements captured in the dilated cost volumes to get the optical flow. In addition to the loss for the optical flow, we design a loss term to better supervise the interpolation weights, leading to better accuracy.

Compared with other approaches, such as PWC-Net [8] and RAFT [12], our approach is conceptually simpler and does not require sequential processing of the cost volumes, as shown in Fig. 1. While obtaining comparable error rates on standard benchmarks, our approach runs significantly faster at inference time, achieving 30 fps (frames per second) for a Sintel-resolution image (with a size of 1024\times 436) on a mid-end 1080ti GPU. Our code and model weights will be made publicly available.
